fatal_errors: The proposed optimum SPS temperature is 950 °C rather than the target 1000 °C, where the reported maximum density, hardness, and environmental resistance occur.
The structural mediator is misidentified as a continuous TiO/TiO2 or Ti-intermetallic grain-boundary network; the target barrier phases are distributed AlV2O4, FeAl2O4, and FeTiO3 oxides.
The oxidation experiment uses 800 °C instead of the specified 900 °C and omits corrosion testing in 3.5 wt% NaCl.
The predicted density above 98% conflicts with the reported optimum of 96.7%, while the hardness prediction above 600 HV fails to reconstruct the measured 1235.5 HV.
The falsification rule compares oxidation rates but does not explicitly distinguish parabolic diffusion control from linear or other surface-reaction-controlled kinetics.
explanation: The response correctly identifies the BCC ball-milled starting state, the role of thermally activated diffusion during SPS, oxygen contamination as a possible source of secondary oxides, and the upper-temperature boundary imposed by Mg volatilization. It also proposes useful TGA and post-mortem TEM/SIMS measurements. However, it selects the wrong optimum temperature, predicts the wrong barrier-phase chemistry, and does not reconstruct the dense passive-film mechanism, biphasic parabolic oxidation behavior, or chloride penetration-defense behavior. The comparison with 1050 °C is useful as a failure control but lies outside the viable processing window. The cited papers support only generic SPS-induced TiO or secondary-phase precipitation in compositionally different alloys; they do not validate a continuous Ti-rich network in Mg-Al-Ti-V-Fe-Co or the quantitative predictions. A decisive experiment should test samples sintered from 850 to 1000 °C, oxidize them at 900 °C, fit separate early- and late-stage parabolic rate constants against linear/interface-controlled models, characterize the oxide-layer stratigraphy and continuity, and pair this with polarization/EIS measurements in 3.5 wt% NaCl.
